clue.text: Flower — one sometimes called Daisy by mistake

parts.note: Daisy is a traditional name for a dairy cow
a slip is a small error

explanation.surface: A flower that people sometimes misname, calling it a daisy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy' looks like another flower, but it is the stock name for a cow; 'by' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The cowslip is a yellow spring wildflower of the primula family.

clue.text: One who ticks off an anti-monarchist?

explanation.surface: Someone who scolds a republican.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ticks off' means marks items as done; the second reading is a chess player who puts the king in check.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone marking items off a list verifies them; a chess player who threatens the opposing king also works against a monarch.

clue.text: Wiser to go without love with the fellow

definitions.text: Wiser to go without love with the fellow

indicators.note: to go without is read as to sit outside, so the first word encloses the others

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written O
the fellow is a man

explanation.surface: Advice that it is smarter to skip romance and stay with the men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go without' sounds like doing without, but it puts WISER around O and MAN. The whole clue also hints at a rake who goes without love.
explanation.definitionFit: A philanderer chases many women without real love, and here is spelt as a man wrapped in wisdom.

clue.text: House matches played here ?

explanation.surface: Wondering where a house plays its games.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Lords is Britain's upper chamber; Lord's in London is the home of cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper chamber of the UK Parliament shares its name with the London cricket ground where Test matches are staged.

clue.text: With opening of public bar maybe get drunk, stewed

indicators.note: opening of picks the first letter of the word after it
maybe signals the letters of the next word in a possible other arrangement

parts.note: oiled is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: When the pub opens, a man might end up sloshed and pickled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges BAR into ARB; 'get' only joins. 'Drunk' and 'stewed' both look like the same sense, but stewed is the cooking definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Parboiling is partial cooking in liquid, close kin to stewing.

clue.text: Gamble in grave situation, French writer lacking capital

parts.note: a tomb is the place where a grave is sited

indicators.note: lacking its capital letter means the writer's name loses its first letter

parts.note: Emile Zola was a French novelist

explanation.surface: Taking a risk in a dire position, like a penniless French author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests money; it means the initial letter, so ZOLA loses its Z to leave OLA.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombola is a raffle-like lottery game, a form of gambling.

clue.text: Traffic, or part of it

explanation.surface: Road congestion, or one piece of it.
explanation.walkthrough: As a noun or verb, truck means trade, dealings; as a lorry it is part of road traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: To have no truck with is to have no dealings, and a lorry is one vehicle in the road traffic.

clue.text: Songs composed by Madam and the girls without them

indicators.note: composed signals that the words are put together in a new order, here once some letters are taken away

explanation.surface: Tunes written by a madam and her girls, without their help.
explanation.walkthrough: Mix MADAM THE GIRLS and take out the letters of THEM ('without them'); the rest rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrigals are part-songs for several voices, popular in Renaissance England.

clue.text: One sort of canoe — Indian, perhaps

indicators.note: one sort of says the word is presented in a different arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A kind of canoe, possibly the Indian type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' looks like describing a canoe; it is the ocean, an example of the definition. 'One sort of' rearranges CANOE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian is one of the world's great seas, given by example.

clue.text: Hot dog

parts.note: not a sausage in a bun but a metal support that sits in the fire

explanation.surface: A frankfurter in a bun.
explanation.walkthrough: Andirons, also called firedogs, are the metal stands that hold logs in a fireplace, so they get hot.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedogs are the iron supports for logs on a hearth, and they sit in the flames.

clue.text: Gantry used by barrel merchant

indicators.note: used by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A lifting frame employed by a cooper's dealer.
explanation.walkthrough: Gantry looks like a crane frame, but it is the surname of Sinclair Lewis's preacher, Elmer Gantry; the first name sits in barrEL MERchant.
explanation.definitionFit: Elmer Gantry is the title character of a Sinclair Lewis novel, so the surname clues his forename.

clue.text: Full supporter of the crown? Far from it

definitions.text: Full supporter of the crown? Far from it

parts.words: Full supporter of the crown? Far from it
parts.note: a crown is also the top of the head, and a full one is round; yet the Civil War faction so nicknamed opposed the king

explanation.surface: A loyal monarchist? Quite the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roundheads were Parliament's side in the English Civil War, named for their cropped hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliamentarians in the English Civil War fought against King Charles I, the very opposite of royalists.

clue.text: He took an all-consuming interest in his subjects

definitions.text: He took an all-consuming interest in his subjects

parts.words: He took an all-consuming interest in his subjects
parts.note: in Aesop's fable the frogs asked for a ruler and got a long-legged bird that ate them up

explanation.surface: A devoted monarch who cared deeply about the people he ruled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All-consuming' sounds like devotion but is literal: the ruler ate his subjects. The answer is given as KING STORK.
explanation.definitionFit: In Aesop's fable of the frogs who wanted a king, Jupiter sends a stork that devours them.

clue.text: Second-best score, a point less than the best

definitions.text: Second-best score, a point less than the best

parts.words: Second-best score, a point less than the best
parts.note: on a shooting target the ring next to the bull scores one fewer than the bull itself

explanation.surface: Coming second in a contest, just one point behind the winner.
explanation.walkthrough: In target shooting the ring just outside the bull's-eye is called the inner.
explanation.definitionFit: On a rifle target the ring round the bull's-eye scores four to the bull's five.

clue.text: They're content in a bed that's comfortable

definitions.text: They're content in a bed that's comfortable

parts.words: They're content in a bed that's comfortable
parts.note: the contents of the proverbial easy bed are garden flowers

explanation.surface: People happily settled in a cosy bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bed of roses' is an idiom for an easy, comfortable situation; 'content' means what the bed contains.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'a bed of roses' names a life of ease, and the flowers fill that flowerbed.

clue.text: Labour active at grass-roots level?

parts.note: not party politics but digging, which literally works where grass has roots

explanation.surface: A political party busy campaigning among ordinary members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' suggests the British political party; here it is toil with a spade, the hard preliminary work.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundwork or hard preparatory toil is so called from digging the soil.

clue.text: For Hobbes the state may provide — I haven't a pound

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from libra

indicators.note: may provide signals that the following words can be reworked to supply new letters

explanation.surface: A plea of poverty: the state may give it, but I'm broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May provide' rearranges IHAVENTA into EVIATHAN, after L. Thomas Hobbes's 1651 treatise names the commonwealth after the biblical sea monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobbes's treatise uses the biblical sea monster as his image of the sovereign commonwealth.

clue.text: Faulty serve, then indecisive ones — little work for linemen

indicators.note: faulty means the word after it is out of order and to be rearranged

parts.note: in tennis a let is a serve that is replayed, giving no decision

explanation.surface: A tennis match of bad serves and lets gives line judges little to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Linemen' are line judges on the surface; here they are poets writing lines. 'Faulty' rearranges SERVE into VERSE; 'then' joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Verselets are short, slight poems, small work for those who write lines.

clue.text: Witch's time to make a call. Fancy!

parts.note: hallo is a call or greeting
ween is an archaic verb meaning to think or suppose

explanation.surface: Time for a witch to make her call, imagine that!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy!' looks like an exclamation of surprise but is the old verb ween, to suppose.
explanation.definitionFit: October 31st is the night traditionally linked with witches.

clue.text: These seeds knocked out in a record upset

indicators.note: upset means the letters of the words in front are knocked over into a new order

explanation.surface: Seeds scattered in a record-breaking upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges the letters of 'in a record'; 'knocked out' only joins, reinforcing the scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: Coriander seeds are a common kitchen spice from the same plant as the herb.

clue.text: Samson's was due to one

parts.note: the hero's downfall came from a haircut, and his fall was a heavy one

explanation.surface: A remark on what brought about Samson's fate.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'come a cropper' is British slang for a heavy fall or failure; Samson fell after Delilah had his hair cropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Samson's ruin followed the cutting of his hair, the work of someone who crops.

clue.text: Only about five succeed at this

indicators.note: about means the first word is placed around the second

parts.note: sole means only, as in the sole survivor
V is the Roman numeral five

explanation.surface: Roughly five people manage to get this right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'approximately' but places SOLE around V. A crossword is the thing solvers succeed at.
explanation.definitionFit: To succeed at a puzzle is to work it out, the self-referential thing every solver does.

clue.text: Where high camp couldn't be higher?

definitions.text: Where high camp couldn't be higher?

parts.words: Where high camp couldn't be higher?
parts.note: camp here is a mountaineers' base, and the highest possible one is on the world's tallest peak

explanation.surface: Flamboyant theatricality at its most extreme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High camp' suggests exaggerated style; it means a climbers' camp on the world's highest mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan summit is the highest point on Earth, so no camp could stand higher.

clue.text: Exercise the right of free speech?

definitions.text: Exercise the right of free speech?

parts.words: Exercise the right of free speech?
parts.note: read literally, using one's freedom to talk means delivering a speech

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone should speak their mind freely.
explanation.walkthrough: The political phrase is read literally: to exercise speech is to make one.
explanation.definitionFit: To declaim or make a formal speech is to use one's voice in public address.

clue.text: I read, in translating, what's published abroad

indicators.note: translating means rendering the letters into another form, a new order

explanation.surface: A reader rendering foreign publications.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' here means widely, not overseas: what is published abroad is broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: To air views is to make them public, spread far and wide.

clue.text: It no longer represents a major achievement

definitions.text: It no longer represents a major achievement

parts.words: It no longer represents a major achievement
parts.note: major means an adult in law; reaching that status once came at a particular birthday that the law has since lowered

explanation.surface: Something that is no longer much of an accomplishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Major' means coming of age: in Britain the age of majority was 21 until 1969, when it became 18. Given as TWENTY-ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Attaining legal adulthood, majority, used to happen at this age before the law lowered it to eighteen.

clue.text: Funny American couple

explanation.surface: A comic pair from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Twain was the American humorist; twain is an old word for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain was the celebrated American humorist, and the archaic word for two names a pair.

clue.text: It shares 20 with a sort of panel

definitions.text: It shares 20 with a sort of panel

parts.words: It shares 20 with a sort of panel
parts.note: the highest peak at 20 lies on a border, and its neighbour's name is a rearranged panel

explanation.surface: Something split with an odd kind of panel.
explanation.walkthrough: Everest (20 down) sits on the border between this region and Nepal, whose letters are PANEL mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan region north of Everest shares the mountain with Nepal.

clue.text: Take someone's place among the jumpers on a team

indicators.note: among says the answer lies within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Replacing a player among the athletes in a jumping squad.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through jumPERS ON A TEam.
explanation.definitionFit: To impersonate or stand in for another is to assume their role.

clue.text: Old note. Always note, read back to front

parts.note: B is a musical note

indicators.note: read back to front says the word for always is spelt in reverse

parts.note: ever means always, as in ever faithful

explanation.surface: A remark about an ancient note, and a reminder to read it backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read back to front' turns EVER into REVE, after B.
explanation.definitionFit: A breve is a long note value of early music, now rarely used.

clue.text: Brave Russian family

parts.note: the Reds was a common name for Russian Communists, taken here in the plural
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: A courageous Russian household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' looks like an adjective but is the old term for a Native American warrior; now considered offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Brave was a dated term for a Native American warrior, and redskin an old, now offensive, word for the same.

clue.text: It's a different catch with this material

indicators.note: different signals the letters of the two words are made into another order

parts.note: to net a fish is to catch it

explanation.surface: A fabric that gives a fresh way of catching something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Different' rearranges ITSA into SATI, then NET follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Satinet is a thin imitation satin cloth.
